content:
The first screen of a service-business homepage should do four jobs in about five seconds: say what you do and for whom, say where you do it, show one believable piece of proof, and offer one obvious next step. Everything else (sliders, mission statements, award badges, three competing buttons) belongs lower down or nowhere. If you are choosing a website designer in Pune, or briefing one, this is the part of the page to argue about first, because it decides whether a visitor from Google or an ad scrolls, calls or leaves.

This guide is written for owners of local service businesses (clinics, coaching classes, interior designers, accountants' offices, repair and installation firms, event planners) who have a homepage that looks fine but does not produce enquiries. It explains what to put in the headline, sub-headline, buttons, image and proof strip; how to build it so it loads fast and works on a phone; how to check it with real visitors; and a handful of patterns that look attractive in a design portfolio but quietly cost you leads.

## What "the first screen" actually means

"Above the fold" is a newspaper term, and on the web it is slippery. A visitor on a 6-inch phone sees roughly the top 600 to 700 pixels of your page before scrolling; someone on a laptop sees more, and someone on a large monitor sees more still. So instead of designing for a fixed line, design for the **first screen on a typical phone**, then let the layout expand gracefully on bigger displays.

Two practical consequences:

1. **Test on a real mid-range Android phone**, not just the browser's device emulator. In India a large share of visitors will be on such devices, often on a mobile connection that varies from room to room.
2. **Anything critical must be visible without scrolling on the phone**: the headline, the main button and at least one trust signal. If your hero image is so tall that the button lands beneath it, the button is effectively hidden.

The first screen is not a place to be clever. Visitors arrive with a question such as "does this firm do what I need, near me, and can I trust it?" The first screen should answer yes or no quickly.

## The five-second test

Before touching design, run this test on your current homepage. Show it to someone who does not know your business, on a phone, for five seconds, then hide it and ask:

- What does this company do?
- Who is it for?
- Where is it based or where does it work?
- What would you do next if you were interested?

If they cannot answer the first three, the first screen is failing, no matter how polished it looks. Keep a note of exactly what they said, because their words are often better headline material than yours.

You can run this test with five or six people in an afternoon. It is not statistically meaningful, and nobody should pretend it is. It is a cheap way to catch an obvious problem before you spend money fixing something else.

## The headline: say what you do, for whom, in plain words

The most common headline mistakes on service websites are:

- **Slogans with no information.** "Excellence in every detail." "Where vision meets reality." A visitor learns nothing.
- **The company name as the headline.** Your name is in the logo already.
- **Clever puns** that a search engine and a stranger cannot parse.

A better formula is: **[what you do] for [who] in [where]**, followed by one benefit or differentiator in the sub-headline.

Worked examples (these are illustrative wording patterns, not claims about any real business):

| Business type | Weak headline | Stronger headline |
|---|---|---|
| Physiotherapy clinic | "Healing with care" | "Physiotherapy clinic in Kothrud, Pune: sports injuries, back pain and post-surgery rehab" |
| Interior designer | "Designing dreams" | "Home interior design in Pune: full flat interiors, planned and delivered by one team" |
| Coaching class | "Shaping futures" | "Class 10 and 12 science coaching in Aundh: small batches, weekly tests, parent updates" |
| AC repair | "Cool solutions" | "AC repair and service in Pune: same-day visits across Baner, Wakad and Hinjewadi" |

Notice what the stronger versions have in common. They name the service in the words a customer would type, they name a place, and they hint at how the business is different. This is also what search engines look for. Your page title, headline and opening paragraph should agree with each other, as covered in our guide to [title tags and meta descriptions](/blog/website-designer-pune-title-tags-meta-descriptions-search-snippets-2026).

Keep the headline to one or two lines on a phone. If it wraps to five lines, it is a paragraph.

### One H1, and it should be this headline

Technically, the homepage should have exactly one H1 element, and the headline above is the natural candidate. Do not make the logo an H1, and do not hide a keyword-stuffed H1 off-screen. The visible headline is the H1. This keeps the page honest for people and clear for search engines.

## The sub-headline: one concrete benefit, one proof of experience

Under the headline, one or two sentences should add what the headline could not fit. Good material includes:

- **How you work:** "Free first visit. Written estimate within two working days." (Only if true.)
- **A verifiable fact:** years in business, number of projects, certifications you hold, professional registrations. Use only figures you can document. If you cannot back a number up, leave it out.
- **Service area:** the neighbourhoods or the radius you cover.

Avoid superlatives such as "best", "number one" or "leading" unless you can cite an independent source. They do not persuade sceptical visitors and can create advertising-claim problems.

## The call to action: one primary button, one secondary

Every first screen needs a **primary action** that matches how your customers actually buy.

- A clinic or salon: "Book an appointment" or "Call now".
- An interior designer or contractor: "Get a free estimate" or "Book a site visit".
- A coaching class: "Book a demo class" or "Download the fee structure".
- An emergency repair service: "Call now", prominent and tappable.

Then at most **one secondary action**, visually quieter, for people who are not ready: "See our work", "WhatsApp us", "View pricing".

Three, four or five equal-weight buttons force the visitor to decide, and a visitor who has to decide often does not. If you have many services, the right answer is a clean services section directly beneath the first screen, not a button for each in the hero.

### Make the buttons honest and tappable

- **Label the action with a verb and an outcome**: "Get a free estimate" beats "Submit" or "Click here".
- **Size for thumbs.** WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum pointer target of 24 by 24 CSS pixels ([W3C Understanding Success Criterion 2.5.8](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html)). A primary button should be considerably larger than the bare minimum, with comfortable space around it.
- **Phone numbers should be real links** (`tel:`) so a tap starts a call, and WhatsApp buttons should open a chat with a sensible pre-filled message. Our guide to [click-to-call and WhatsApp buttons](/blog/website-designer-pune-click-to-call-whatsapp-buttons-mobile-service-website-2026) covers the details and the tracking.
- **Do not hide the button behind a popup or an animation delay.** If it appears three seconds late, some visitors will already have scrolled away.

## The hero image: real, relevant, light

The image beside or behind the headline carries more emotional weight than any sentence on the page, and it is where many Pune service sites lose trust: a stock photo of smiling people in a glass-walled office that is obviously not in Pune.

Principles that hold up:

- **Prefer real photographs of your team, premises or completed work.** Visitors are quick to spot stock imagery, and for a local business, a real photo of the actual clinic entrance or a finished kitchen is evidence.
- **Show the outcome or the service happening**, not a generic mood shot.
- **If you must use stock, choose images with no obviously foreign context** (street signs, uniforms, car number plates, power sockets), and do not pretend they are your premises.
- **Get consent for photos of people**, especially patients, students and children. Never show a client's face without permission.
- **Keep the file light.** The hero image is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, which Google measures as part of Core Web Vitals; a good LCP is 2.5 seconds or less at the 75th percentile of visits ([web.dev: Largest Contentful Paint](https://web.dev/articles/lcp)). Serve a correctly sized, compressed AVIF or WebP version and give it explicit width and height so the layout does not jump; our guide to [image optimisation with AVIF and WebP](/blog/website-designer-pune-image-optimization-avif-webp-lcp-2026) shows how.
- **Never lazy-load the hero image.** Lazy loading is for images below the first screen. Loading the hero late delays the very thing visitors are waiting for.

Skip full-screen autoplay video backgrounds unless you have a clear reason and a tested lightweight implementation. They are heavy on mobile data, can distract from the message, and are rarely what turns a visitor into an enquiry.

## The proof strip: one line of reasons to believe you

Directly under or beside the buttons, a slim strip of proof reassures the visitor who is deciding whether to trust you with money or their home. Pick from what you genuinely have:

- **A review summary** you can link to, such as your Google rating and review count, linking to your actual Google Business Profile. Quote the numbers exactly as shown there on the day you publish, and update them. Do not round up, and do not mark up your own reviews as review stars; Google's guidance does not allow self-serving review markup for local businesses. Our guide on [testimonials and review schema](/blog/website-designer-pune-testimonials-reviews-section-review-schema-2026) explains the boundary.
- **Registrations and memberships** that are relevant and verifiable: a medical council registration, a professional body, a trade licence.
- **Recognisable client or project types**, only with permission.
- **Years of operation**, if you can state them accurately.
- **A guarantee or policy** you actually honour, in plain words.

Three items are plenty. A wall of logos, badges and award graphics reads as noise, and invented or unverifiable badges are worse than none.

## Local signals: let a Pune visitor know you are in Pune

For a local business, the first screen should make location unmistakable, without cramming "Pune" into every line:

- Mention the city or neighbourhood naturally in the headline or sub-headline.
- Show a **visible address and opening hours** in the header or just below the hero, or one tap away from it on mobile.
- If customers visit you, a "Get directions" link to Google Maps is as valuable as a phone button.
- Keep your name, address and phone number consistent with your Google Business Profile and with your [LocalBusiness structured data](/blog/web-development-company-pune-localbusiness-schema-nap-opening-hours-2026).

Do not create a hero that claims to serve "all of Maharashtra" if you realistically serve three suburbs. Overstating your area attracts the wrong enquiries and weakens the local relevance Google looks for.

## Navigation on the first screen

The header menu competes with your headline. Some rules of thumb:

- **Five to seven top-level items** is usually plenty for a small service site: Services, About, Work (or Reviews), Pricing, Contact.
- **Do not hide the main menu behind a hamburger on desktop.** On mobile, a hamburger is normal, but keep the phone or WhatsApp button visible beside it.
- **Make the logo link to the homepage**, and keep the header small so it does not eat the first screen. A sticky header that covers a third of a phone screen is a hidden cost; if you make it sticky, make it slim.
- **Match the menu words to customer language.** "Our Expertise" is worse than "Services".

## Build notes: what a developer should do

A good first screen is partly design and partly engineering. For your developer, a short checklist:

1. **One H1** with the headline; logical H2s for the sections below.
2. **Hero image**: correct dimensions, modern format, `fetchpriority="high"` on the element when it is the LCP image, and no lazy loading.
3. **Fonts**: use one or two font families, preload only the critical weight, and set `font-display` sensibly to avoid invisible text. See our note on [web fonts and layout shift](/blog/website-designer-pune-web-fonts-font-display-layout-shift-2026), including how to handle Devanagari text if your site is bilingual.
4. **No layout shift**: reserve space for the image, banner and cookie notice so buttons do not move as the page loads. A moving button causes mis-taps.
5. **No slider carousel** for the main message. Carousels hide most of their slides from most visitors, and the first slide must carry the message anyway; if you need several messages, show them as separate sections.
6. **Contrast**: text must be readable on the image, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text under WCAG ([W3C Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html)). Put a solid or semi-opaque panel behind text rather than relying on a photo's quiet corner.
7. **Cookie and consent banners** should not cover the main button on a phone. See our guide to [cookie consent banners](/blog/web-development-company-pune-cookie-consent-banner-block-scripts-dpdp-2026).
8. **Tracking**: tag the main button, the phone link and the WhatsApp link as key events so you can see which one produces enquiries; our guide to [GA4 key events for forms, calls and WhatsApp](/blog/web-development-company-pune-ga4-key-events-form-call-whatsapp-lead-tracking-2026) explains the setup.

## A worked example: rewriting a weak first screen

Here is a hypothetical before-and-after for an invented interior design studio, to show the reasoning. (The business and the wording are illustrative; none of the claims are real.)

**Before:**

- Headline: "Creating Spaces You Love"
- Sub-headline: "Welcome to Studio Aria, where creativity meets craftsmanship."
- Buttons: "Home", "About", "Portfolio", "Services", "Blog", "Contact" in the hero; a slider of six full-width photos; an autoplay video in the background.
- Proof: none visible.

**Problems:** the visitor learns the studio name and nothing else; no service, no place, no next step, no proof; heavy media on mobile.

**After:**

- Headline: "Full-home interior design in Pune"
- Sub-headline: "One team for design, carpentry and finishing. Free site visit and a written scope before you pay anything." (Only valid if that is the studio's actual offer.)
- Primary button: "Book a free site visit"
- Secondary button: "See completed homes"
- Proof strip: "4.8 on Google (62 reviews)" with a link to the profile, as an example of how a verifiable rating would be shown; "Member, [relevant trade body]" if true.
- Image: a real photograph of a finished living room from the studio's own project, compressed, with the heading text on a dark panel.
- Location: "Studio at [address], Pune. Open Mon-Sat" with a map link.

Nothing here required a bigger budget. It required deciding what to say and in what order.

## How to check that the new first screen works

Do not judge by taste or by what the loudest person in the meeting prefers. Use evidence:

1. **Five-second test** again, with fresh people.
2. **Real-device test** on a mid-range Android phone and an iPhone, on mobile data, in daylight.
3. **PageSpeed Insights** for the real-user Core Web Vitals data when your site has enough traffic, and lab data when it does not.
4. **Search Console** for the queries and pages that bring visitors, so the headline matches what people actually search for.
5. **Session recordings and heatmaps** from a privacy-respecting tool to see where visitors tap and where they stall; see our guide to [Clarity heatmaps and session recordings](/blog/website-designer-pune-clarity-heatmaps-session-recordings-enquiries-2026). Mask forms and tell visitors in your privacy notice.
6. **Enquiry counts** by source over several weeks. A small business may get few enquiries a week, so avoid conclusions from a handful of days. If you want to run a formal comparison with low traffic, read our note on [A/B testing a landing page with little traffic](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-landing-page-ab-testing-low-traffic-2026).

Change one thing at a time where you can, write down the date of each change, and give it long enough to see a pattern.

## Things that look good in a portfolio and cost you leads

- **Parallax and heavy scroll effects** that stutter on mid-range phones.
- **Hero text over a busy photo** with low contrast.
- **Auto-rotating sliders** that move before visitors finish reading.
- **A splash screen or intro animation** that makes visitors wait before they can do anything.
- **Chat widgets that cover the call button** on small screens.
- **"Scroll down" arrows** as a substitute for a clear message.
- **Pop-ups within seconds of landing**, especially full-screen ones on mobile, which frustrate visitors and can attract search penalties for intrusive interstitials.
- **Buried contact details**: a phone number only in the footer.

None of these is forbidden, but each should earn its place with a clear reason and a test.

## When to hire a website designer in Pune, and what to ask for

If you hire a website designer, ask to see the first screen of two or three comparable sites they built, on a phone, and ask what they learned from them. Ask:

- How will you decide the headline, and will you test it with real people?
- How will the first screen behave on a mid-range Android phone on mobile data?
- Which buttons will be tracked as key events, and who will look at the results?
- Who owns the photographs, fonts and licensed assets afterwards?

A designer who answers in terms of visitors and enquiries is thinking about the right problem. One who answers only in terms of trends and animations may deliver a beautiful page that does not work as a sales tool.

## Frequently asked questions

### What should be on the first screen of a business homepage?
A clear headline saying what you do, for whom and where; a one- or two-sentence sub-headline; one primary button that matches how customers buy; one real image; and a short proof strip such as a verifiable review summary or registration. Keep everything else lower on the page.

### How long does a visitor spend deciding whether to stay?
There is no single reliable number, and you should be wary of claims that quote one. What matters is that a first-time visitor can answer what you do, where, and what to do next within a few seconds. Test this with real people on a phone rather than relying on a statistic.

### Should a homepage use a slider or carousel?
Generally no for the main message. Sliders show one slide at a time, most visitors never see the others, and they add weight and complexity. Present your main message once, clearly, and give other messages their own sections.

### Is a video background good for a service website?
Rarely. Autoplay video is heavy on mobile data, can slow the Largest Contentful Paint, and often distracts from the call to action. If video genuinely helps, such as a short clip of your work, host it efficiently, load it after the main content, and do not autoplay with sound.

### How do I know if my homepage headline is working?
Look at whether visitors take the main action. Track clicks on the primary button, phone and WhatsApp links and form submissions as key events, and compare enquiry numbers across several weeks. Pair this with a five-second test using people who do not know your business.
